previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman was admitted for worsening bilateral leg pain, redness, and swelling, initially concerning for cellulitis, but found to be due to chronic lymphedema with venous stasis changes. Despite prior outpatient treatment with IV furosemide and clindamycin, her symptoms progressed, prompting hospitalization for diuresis and infection evaluation. IV vancomycin was started but discontinued after no improvement and negative blood cultures, with dermatology attributing findings to stasis. A CT scan ruled out abdominal masses but revealed new renal lesions requiring outpatient MRI follow-up. Diuresis with IV furosemide and metolazone was limited by rising creatinine, leading to discontinuation. She was treated for sinusitis with levofloxacin and oral thrush with nystatin. Her INR was optimized on warfarin, and a brief non-epileptic event was noted. She was discharged home with services on oral diuretics, with instructions to monitor weight, follow up with her PCP, and complete imaging for renal lesions.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ yo F with a complex PMH significant for chronic ___ lymphedema 
and recurrent cellulitis with recent L back corticosteroid 
injection who presents with likely shingles in L T3/4 dermatomal 
distribution with RLE cellulitis. New zoster lesions in 
non-adjacent dermatomes occurred during admission, so she was 
treated with 10 day course of IV acyclovir due to concern for 
disseminated zoster. Cellulitis was initially treated with IV 
clindamycin with marked improvement in less than 24 hours. 
Switched to PO Keflex after confirmation with the patient that 
she tolerated this antibiotic in the past; however switched back 
to clindamycin as cellulitis was not improving. Patient was 
having severe pain from her zoster requiring IV dilaudid for 
breakthrough. She was transitioned to oral dilaudid PRN in a 
dose equivalent with her home oxycodone in an attempt to wean of 
IV narcotics. Yellow ulcerated tongue lesion seen during 
admission, unclear etiology (oral ___ vs. trauma/bite) but 
was evaluated by ENT who had low suspicion for cancer. She was 
restarted on her home diuretics following her course of 
acyclovir. Wound care was consulted for blistering on bilateral 
legs secondary to fluid overload.

ACTIVE ISSUES: 
==========================
# Disseminated zoster: Pt initially presented with L T3/T4 
dermatomal reactivation zoster. New lesions in non-adjacent 
dermatomes seen ___, confirmed disseminated zoster with 
scrape biopsy ___. No sign of visceral organ involvement, 
LFTs ___ WNL. No known reason for immunocompromise (see below). 
Pt placed on airborne isolation precautions and given 10 day 
course of IV acyclovir with pre- and post-hydration. Pt 
complained of R earache and bilateral eye 
pain/blurriness/tearing, concerning for zoster 
oticus/ophthalmicus. Was evaluated by ID and ophtho who had low 
suspicion for trigeminal nerve involvement. No new lesions seen 
at time of discharge. 

# Cellulitis: Patient with chronic ___ lymphedema on chronic 
suppressive therapy with doxycycline, presented with cellulitis 
in RLE. She received clindamycin in the ED. Has usually received 
clindamycin for past cellulitis, but gets oral thrush. Was 
switched to Keflex on floor. However, cellulitis appeared 
worsened and along with elevated WBC, decided to switch to 7 day 
course of clindamycin 600 mg Q6 PO. Appeared to be resolved by 
time of discharge.

# Tongue lesion: Painful, yellow, ulcerated tongue lesion noted 
___. Unclear history as to how long it has been there. Has h/o 
thrush when taking clindamycin, was on Nystatin for prophylaxis. 
However, pt reports this is not like her usual episodes of 
thrush. Pt was started on fluconazole and was evaluated by ENT 
___, who thought the lesion was likely a healing laceration 
from possibly having bitten her tongue. No underlying firm or 
indurated lesion that would be more concerning for malignancy. 
Stopped fluconazole as the lesion appeared to be healing and 
atypical presentation for oral ___. ENT recommended 
outpatient f/u in ___ weeks.

# Immunocompromise/infectious w/u: Pt has h/o recurrent 
cellulitis, infections, oral thrush and now has disseminated 
zoster despite no known reason to be immunocompromised. HIV 
viral load not detected, absolute CD4 count 840 (___), RPR 
negative, HTLV-1 negative, Histoplasma Ag negative. No reason to 
believe that the patient is immunocompromised.

# Acute on chronic lower extremity edema and venous stasis: Pt 
has chronic severe lower extremity edema and venous stasis which 
worsened in the setting of additional fluid boluses for 
acyclovir. Home diuresis regimen consists of Bumex 1 mg 5x/week 
and Lasix 8 ml IV 2 times a week as needed for edema per OMR, 
but was held as inpatient ___ concern for renal damage. Pt was 
given IV Lasix before being restarted on her home bumex 1 mg. 
She developed blistering in her legs secondary to edema and a 
wound care consult was obtained. She was given supplies and 
instructions for wound care at discharge. Weight on discharge 
was 159.3  kg, admission weight was not obtained. 

# Pain control: Pt has fibromyalgia and chronic ___ lymphedema 
and takes narcotics at home. During admission, patient was often 
sleepy, appearing to doze off during interviews and reportedly 
falling asleep on the toilet, yet asked for escalation of pain 
control. Did not believe it was safe to further escalate pain 
control and transitioned from IV to PO Dilaudid. Restarted her 
home narcotic regimen for breakthrough pain, but never required 
immediate release morphine and instructions were to not take 
this while at home.

# History of DVT w/ PE: Continued Coumadin with MD dosing daily 
with goal INR 2.0-3.0. Course of fluconazole complicated dosing 
of Coumadin. Sent out on 6 mg daily with instructions to check 
INR in next week and adjust Coumadin as needed.

CHRONIC ISSUES: 
==========================
# Seizure disorder: Pt has never had documented seizures, has 
past diagnosis of PNES. Tongue ulcer (see above) potentially 
from bite but unlikely given that there was no bleeding and the 
ulceration has occurred slowly over the course of this 
hospitalization. Patient also has not had bladder incontinence 
that would be expected with the classic tonic clonic seizure. 
Continued home Keppra and Topamax.
# HTN: Continued home meds.
# HLD: Continued home ezetimibe.
# Fibromyalgia: Continued home gabapentin and opioid pain 
medications.
# Hypothyroidism: Continued home levothyroxine.

This test is approved for monitoring HIV-1 viral load in known HIV-positive patients. It is not approved for diagnosis of acute HIV infection.  In symptomatic acute HIV infection (acute retroviral syndrome), the viral load is usually very high (>>1000 copies/mL). If acute HIV infection is clinically suspected and there is a detectable but low viral load, please contact the laboratory for interpretation.  It is recommended that any NEW positive HIV-1 viral load result, in the absence of positive serology, be confirmed by submitting a new sample FOR HIV-1 PCR, in addition to serological testing.
